## Methods

Materials
Unless stated otherwise, materials and solvents were commercially obtained. PM6, Y6, D18, N3, L8-BO, P3HT and other conjugated organic small molecules and polymers were purchased from Solmer Materials Inc. All materials were used as received without further purification.

Reflection measurement
1.5 cm × 1.5 cm size quartz was pre-cleaned with ultrasonic in deionized water, acetone and isopropyl alcohol for three times, 10 min each, then dried with Argon blow. The active layer was spin-coated in air condition from a chloroform (CF) or o-dichlorobenzene (o-DCB) solution of Y6(P3HT) which was prepared with the concentration of 10 mg/ml. The thickness of the Y6(P3HT) active layer was optimized as 40 nm (60 nm). The thermal annealing step was carried out in air, and the annealing temperatures of Y6 and P3HT were 160°C and 200°C, respectively. The reflection measurement was performed by a self-built setup which was composed with a Y-shape optical fiber and a grating spectrometer. Finally, the reflection results were revised by a standard Aluminum mirror. To accelerate the speed of the spectrometer, a fast CCD detector is used, which guaranteed that the optical reflection at each wavelength was simultaneously recorded. For each spectrum, the capture time could be tuned towards less than a few milliseconds.

Refraction measurement
Spectral data below 1.7 µm were measured using an RC2 ellipsometer to obtain the ellipsometric parameters Ψ and Δ. The measurements were performed at angles ranging from 45° to 60° in 5° increments. The dielectric function was extracted by fitting the ellipsometric parameters using a B-Spline oscillator model. For wavelengths above 1.7 µm, an IR-VASE Mark II ellipsometer was used, with measurements taken at 60° and 70° at a resolution of 8 cm−1. The dielectric function was obtained by fitting the ellipsometric parameters (Ψ and Δ) using three Lorentz oscillators. The sample preparation for the ellipsometer measurement are the same as for reflection measurement.

Device preparation
The conventional devices were fabricated with a structure of glass/ITO/PEDOT:PSS/active layers/PNDIT-F3N/Ag. The ITO-coated glass substrates were cleaned by ultrasonic treatment in detergent, deionized water, acetone, and isopropyl alcohol under ultrasonication for 15 min each and subsequently dried by a nitrogen blow. A thin layer (~20 nm) of PEDOT:PSS (Clevios P VP AI 4083, filtered at 0.45 μm) was spin-coated at 4000 rpm onto ITO surface. After baked at 150°C for 20 min, the substrates were transferred into a nitrogen-filled glovebox. Subsequently, the blend solution of PM6:Y6 (1:1.2 w/w, from CF with 0.5% CN), PM6:L8-BO (1:1.2 w/w, from CF with 0.25% DIO) or D18:N3 (1:1 w/w, from CF) was spin-coated to form the active layers with different thicknesses. Then the substrates were TA treatment with 100°C for 5 min. After that, The ETL solution PNDIT-F3N was spin-coated on the top of active layers at 3000 rpm. Finally, 120 nm Ag layer were deposited under high vacuum (<1.5×10−4 Pa). The effective areas of cells were ~4 mm2 defined by shallow masks.

The inverted devices were fabricated with a structure of glass/ITO/ZnO/active layer/MoO 3/Ag. A ZnO sol-gel solution was deposited onto pre-treated ITO-coated glass substrates via spin-coating, followed by annealing on a hot plate at 200°C for 30 min to form an ~30 nm-thick electron transport layer. Subsequently, a CF solution of the prepared PM6:Y6 blend active layer was spin-coated onto the ZnO layer. By adjusting the concentration and spin speed, thin films with different thicknesses were fabricated, which were then annealed on a hotplate at 100°C for 5 min. The sample was then transferred into a vacuum deposition chamber, where ~8 nm of MoO 3 and 120 nm of Ag metal electrodes were thermally evaporated sequentially under high vacuum conditions (<1.5×10−4 Pa). The effective areas of cells were ~4 mm2 defined by shallow masks.

The fabrication process for flexible PM6:Y6 devices was consistent with that of conventional devices, except that the substrate was replaced with ITO-coated PET substrates.

Device characterization
The J–V curves of all devices were recorded by a Keithley 2400 source meter and a simulated AM 1.5G (100 mW/cm−2) solar spectrum generating from LSS-55 solar simulator (50×50 mm2 spot size) of Jinzhu Technology CO., LTD.

The EQE spectral were recorded utilizing spectral response measurement system LST-QE of Jinzhu Technology CO., LTD.

Ultrafast recombination characterization
Femtosecond transient absorption (fs-TA) spectroscopy (Coherent Legend) was conducted with a wavelength of 800 nm and a laser of 2840 mW (80 MHz, 120 fs) emitted from a seed source through a titanium sapphire amplifier. The laser wavelength is still 800 nm, the pulse is 1000 Hz, the time interval is 120 fs. 30% of the beam is used as the probe enters the transient absorption spectrometer, and the remaining 70% is converted to 400 nm by BBO crystal, which is pumped into the sample as excitation light (400 nm, 1000 Hz, 100 mW). The test section is the visible light region (450–800 nm).

Transient photovoltage (TPV)/transient photocurrent (TPC)
The TPV and TPC data were acquired with the all-in-one characterization platform Paios (Fluxim AG, Switzerland). In the TPV measurement, the light intensity is in the range of 0.10% to 80.0%, the relative intensity is 20.0%, the stabilization time is 30.0 ms, and the pulse length is 5.0 ms. The TPC of the device was tested under short-circuit conditions without bias light.

GIWAXS measurement
GIWAXS data were collected at beamline BL14B1 of the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility (SSRF). The wavelength was 1.2398 Å and the incident angle was 0.12o.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

Shen and coworkers systematically investigate the intrinsic light reflection characteristics of organic conjugated thin films and their impact on the performance of organic photovoltaic devices. Through GIWAXS experiments and TD-DFT theoretical calculations, they found that the electronic polarizability and molecular stacking orientation of organic semiconductor materials are the key factors determining their high reflectivity (up to 50%). Further researches show that by regulating film thickness and molecular orientation, microcavity effects can be optimized, thereby improving the performance of OSCs. Through analyzing the four stages of the effect of film thickness on the reflection situation, the author clarified the differences in reflection sources and light loss levels under different film thicknesses, and based on this, proposed a solution to synergistically enhance material polarizability and face-on orientation to improve the material’s refractive index. In addition, the authors verified their strategy in different material systems (PM6:Y6, D18:N3). This work focuses on the important but rarely discussed issue of light reflection in organic photovoltaic devices, and further analyzes the sources, effects, and optimization methods of light reflection, which are crucial for the further development of OSCs. However, whether light reflection has such a significant effect still requires more evidence to support it; therefore, I recommend its publication in Nature Communications after major revision. Here are my comments:
1.The author explored the reflectivity of 1D and 2D materials separately. What is the classification basis for them? Electronic polarizability or other factors? Actually, the polymers such as PM6 were designed based on the method of 2D conjugate extension.
2.In the first part of the high reflection of 1D- and 2D-conjugated molecules, very high reflection values were found for Y6 and P3HT-based films. However, in the device characterization part, the reflection values are missing. To illustrate the real effect of reflection on device performance, the author should comprehensively analyze light utilization in devices, including the interrelationships between EQE, reflection, and transmission, to quantitatively explain the impact of reflection.
3.The effect of conjugated film intrinsic light reflection on device performance should be universally applicable in different device architectures, such as inverted, flexible, and LBL devices. The corresponding characterization and analysis should be conducted.
4.This manuscript is titled “Intrinsic Light Reflection of Conjugated 1 Films towards Organic Optoelectronics”, while only OSC material and device are involved and discussed. How about OLED and OPD? Are the conclusions still universally valid?
5.There are several minor errors throughout the manuscript, such as the Y6 structure in Fig. 1. Please review and revise accordingly.

### Reviewer 2

The work by Shen et al. studied the impact of active layer thickness and optical constant on the light management of organic photovoltaics. The four stages they proposed rationalized the thickness-dependent Jsc of OPVs in a straightforward manner, providing effective strategies for future performance optimization. While many previous works claimed that thick-film OPVs are required to achieve full absorption of the solar spectrum, this work pointed out that a thin active layer is more desirable in NFA-based OPVs, as the 2D conjugation of NFAs leads to a much higher refractive index compared to traditional 1D homopolymers like P3HT. Therefore, I think this work is suitable for publication in Nature Communications after revising the following issues.
1. In lines 222-225 of the manuscript, the authors assigned the in-plane diffraction peaks of Y6 at 0.28 Å-1 and 0.42 Å-1 to the (001) and (100) peaks, corresponding to periodic packings along the backbone (the long axis of conjugated backbone) and the lamellar (the short axis of conjugated backbone) directions, respectively, as illustrated in Fig. 2. Such assignment is incorrect. In previous work by Xiao et al. [Journal of Materials Chemistry A, 2021, 9(31): 17030-17038.], both peaks were assigned to the second and third order diffraction along the backbone direction. In two other works [Nature communications, 2020, 11(1): 3943.] and [Advanced Energy Materials, 2020, 10(18): 1904234.], those two peaks were also assigned to periodic packings along the backbone direction of Y6 molecules, although they were referred to as ‘lamellar stackings’. Therefore, while it is reasonable to claim that the molecular orientation order improves upon thermal annealing, the detailed peak assignment should be revised.
2. In lines 259-262 of the manuscript, the author defined the 2D orientation parameter S2D as 2cos(2γ)-1. However, based on the paper they referred to [Chemistry of Materials, 2020, 32(14): 6043-6054], S2D should be defined as 2cos2(γ)-1. Please check.
3. In lines 368-372 of the manuscript, the authors claimed that the shunt resistance (Rsh) of the device peaks at 75 nm and decreases as the thickness is further increased to 220 nm. This is unexpected as thicker devices typically show higher Rsh. It should be noted that Rsh should be determined from the inverse differential of the dark J-V curve at 0 V [Advanced Energy Materials, 2016, 6(11): 1502250.]. On the other hand, Rsh extracted from the light J-V curve takes into account the transport resistance of photo-generated charge carriers [Nature Communications, 2015, 6(1): 6951], which no longer reflects the true shunt resistance of the device. Similarly, series resistance should also be obtained from the dark J-V curve. The authors should include the experimental procedure they employed to measure Rs and Rsh to avoid misinterpretation.
4. In lines 414-417 of the manuscript, the authors claimed that the reflection primarily takes place at the HTL/active layer interface and the ETL/Ag interface, where the difference in refractive index (n) is the largest. The authors should include the wavelength-dependent values of n for all layers involved in OPVs for better illustration.
5. It should be noted that the optical length difference between R1 and T2 is 2nd rather than nd. Therefore, the condition of the first destructive interference, as noted in Fig. 6c of the manuscript, should be d = λ/4n rather than d = λ/2n.

### Reviewer 3

In this study, the intrinsic reflection characteristics of organic conjugated films are systematically investigated to elucidate their impact on the optical properties and performance of organic solar cells (OSCs). The authors reveal that the polarizability of 2D conjugated molecules and their face-on orientation determine the intrinsic reflectance of organic films (up to 52 %). Due to the microcavity interference effect, the PM6:Y6-based devices exhibit a maximum short-circuit current density (JSC) at a thickness of approximately 75 nm. Furthermore, the authors experimentally and computationally demonstrate that the microcavity effect and optical interference are key factors driving variations in device performance such as JSC, and they propose a performance optimization strategy based on molecular polarizability and backbone orientation. However, several points need to be addressed to improve the quality of the manuscript and to provide a more comprehensive perspective.
1. The manuscript lacks a systematic analysis of how device performance and film properties vary under different solvent systems (e.g., chloroform, chlorobenzene) and thermal annealing conditions. It would strengthen the study if the authors could justify their choice of specific solvent and annealing parameters or discuss whether alternative conditions were considered.
2. The manuscript proposes two key strategies-enhancing molecular polarizability and maximizing face-on packing-for improving device performance. Could the authors clarify whether these two strategies can be simultaneously achieved in practice, and whether there are any potential trade-offs or conflicting aspects between them?
3. While the study focuses on optical optimization for enhanced device performance, it would be valuable to discuss how such optimization strategies might affect the long-term durability and stability of the devices. Could the authors comment on any potential implications in this regard?

Here are my comments:

Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting this important issue. The 1D- and 2D- polarized materials were distinguished according to the polarizability direction of the materials films. Although donor polymers like PM6 possess 2D conjugated molecular segments, they exhibit quasi-1D polarized characteristics due to superior electron delocalization along the polymer backbone direction. Furthermore, the predominantly edge-on/isotropic molecular stacking orientation of PM6-type polymer donors aligns their yy-polarization direction perpendicular to the substrate plane—orthogonal to the electric field vector of incident light (https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.202509532). Consequently, yy-direction polarization remains largely unexcited under standard illumination conditions, thereby exhibiting optical behavior analogous to 1D- polarized systems. This is experimentally evidenced by their comparable maximum reflectivity to 1D- polarized polymers (e.g., P3HT), which remains significantly lower than that of 2D- polarized molecules (e.g., Y6) featuring face-on stacking orientations.
We have added “In fact, polymer donor materials such as PM6 and PBDB-T possess a certain degree of two-dimensional polarizability based on their molecular structures. Nevertheless, they exhibit optical constants nearly identical in magnitude to those of one-dimensionally polarized molecules like P3HT. This phenomenon arises partly because their two-dimensional polarizability is less pronounced than that of molecules with extensive two-dimensional conjugation, such as Y6. Additionally, they tend to adopt an edge-on/isotropic molecular packing orientation, where the molecular y-axis is perpendicular to the electric field vector of incident light. Consequently, polarization along the y-direction remains inactivated. 2.In the first part of the high reflection of 1D- and 2D-conjugated molecules, very high reflection values were found for Y6 and P3HT-based films. Response: Thank you for pointing this out. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 17, we measured the total reflection spectra of PM6:Y6 devices with varying active-layer thicknesses and convolved these spectra with the AM1.5G solar irradiance profile to evaluate the light loss fraction, which aligns well with our simulation results. As evidenced by Supplementary Fig. 17 and Fig. 5b, the overall device reflection is substantially lower than that measured from the bare active-layer film, which primarily stems from the optical behavior at the R interface (defined in Fig. 5a). Conversely, in bare active-layer HTL measurements, R represents the active-layer/air interface with a large difference (n ≈ 1 air 1), resulting in significantly stronger reflection. Furthermore, through strategic thickness optimization, the Y6 film exhibiting maximum reflection was engineered at ~50 nm. At this thickness, constructive interference enhances the T component (i.e., 2 the second-pass reflected light), thereby amplifying the overall reflected intensity. Additionally, we provide an in-depth discussion correlating the interplay among EQE, reflection, and transmission on page 19, Supplementary Information.
“Theoretically, due to the presence of the Ag electrode, OSC devices are opaque (T = 0). Therefore, the wavelength-dependent characteristics of the device reflection spectra should correspond to the EQE measurement results: stronger reflection light at a specific wavelength leads to a weaker EQE signal, and vice versa. Accordingly, we compared the reflection spectra with the EQE for devices of different thicknesses (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 17). However, the reported layer-by-layer (LBL) processed devices still possess a BHJ region at the donor/acceptor interface, and the vertical phase separation observed in the BHJ region can influence optical absorption and may significantly interfere with the thickness-dependent behavior of J . Additionally, during the sequential coating SC process of the active layer (especially spin-coating), due to the use of incompletely orthogonal solvents, the second coating step will cause mass loss in the initially deposited layer, resulting in uncertainty in the donor-acceptor composition. Compared to LBL devices, we believe that inverted and flexible BHJ devices are sufficient to validate the observed phenomena and the reliability of the proposed optical model. Therefore, we conducted the same investigations on inverted and flexible devices as on conventional devices, and the results are shown in Supplementary Figs. 18-20. We have also added the following explanation on page 20 of the main text.
“In addition to conventional forward devices, we also conducted identical studies on inverted devices with different transport layers and electrodes, as well as flexible devices with different substrates, using the PM6:Y6 system as an example. The device performance test results are shown in Supplementary Fig. 18 and Supplementary Table 3. It can be observed that both inverted and flexible devices exhibit a similar trend of J variation with thickness as conventional devices (Fig. 5), indicating that minor SC differences in the optical constants of the transport layers, electrodes, and substrates do not significantly affect the optical performance of the devices (Supplementary Fig. 19). This conclusion is further supported by the experimental and simulated light absorption results of PM6:Y6 inverted devices with different thicknesses (Supplementary Fig. 20).”

Reviewer 3
Comments: In this study, the intrinsic reflection characteristics of organic conjugated films are systematically investigated to elucidate their impact on the optical properties and performance of organic solar cells (OSCs). The authors reveal that the polarizability of 2D conjugated molecules and their face-on orientation determine the intrinsic reflectance of organic films (up to 52 %). Due to the microcavity interference effect, the PM6:Y6-based devices exhibit a maximum short-circuit current density (JSC) at a thickness of approximately 75 nm. Furthermore, the authors experimentally and computationally demonstrate that the microcavity effect and optical interference are key factors driving variations in device performance such as JSC, and they propose a performance optimization strategy based on molecular polarizability and backbone orientation. However, several points need to be addressed to improve the quality of the manuscript and to provide a more comprehensive perspective.
Response: We sincerely appreciate your thorough evaluation and constructive feedback. Below are our point-by-point responses to the key concerns raised.
1. The manuscript lacks a systematic analysis of how device performance and film properties vary under different solvent systems (e.g., chloroform, chlorobenzene) and thermal annealing conditions. It would strengthen the study if the authors could justify their choice of specific solvent and annealing parameters or discuss whether alternative conditions were considered.
Response: We appreciate this important observation. Regarding the systems discussed in the manuscript, taking PM6:Y6 as an example, our preparation method largely follows most reported literature protocols: spin-coating from chloroform (CF) solution at room temperature followed by thermal annealing at 100℃ for 5 minutes (literature typically reports annealing between 90-110℃). Firstly, CF was selected as the solvent because chlorobenzene (CB) has a higher boiling point and slower evaporation rate, which promotes the formation of larger crystalline domains of Y6 (and its derivatives) in the film. This coarsened morphology restricts the formation of a nanoscale interpenetrating network, thereby reducing charge generation efficiency. In contrast, chloroform’s lower boiling point enables faster solvent evaporation, limiting further crystal growth of Y6 and facilitating the development of an interpenetrating donor-acceptor nanomorphology. Our early work attempted CB as solvent but yielded unsatisfactory performance [Adv. Mater. Interfaces 2020, 7, 2000577]. However, an alternative approach using CB is possible through hot spin-coating. For D18, which exhibits extremely poor solubility in CF but dissolves well in hot CB solutions, hot spin-coating with CB at elevated temperatures allows rapid solvent evaporation due to the high temperature, thereby restricting excessive growth of NFA crystals. The D18:Y6 devices in this study were fabricated via hot spin-coating at 80℃ using CB as solvent. Similarly, excessively high annealing temperatures can also promote further growth of Y6 crystals. For instance, annealing above 200℃ leads to micron-scale crystal formation, severely disrupting the film morphology. Even annealing at 160°C, while not causing significant micron-scale phase separation, still damages the nanoscale interpenetrating network. Device performance is highly sensitive to such morphological degradation. Therefore, following common literature practice, our study employs 100 ℃ thermal annealing.
We have added a brief explanation “To this end, a series of PM6:Y6 blend films with thicknesses ranging from 20 nm to 200 nm were fabricated using chloroform as the solvent and subsequently subjected to TA treatment at 100℃ for 5 minutes” on Page 12 to clarify our rationale for selecting chloroform and 100℃ annealing as the preparation conditions for PM6:Y6 devices.
2. The manuscript proposes two key strategies-enhancing molecular polarizability and maximizing face-on packing-for improving device performance. Could the authors clarify whether these two strategies can be simultaneously achieved in practice, and whether there are any potential trade-offs or conflicting aspects between them?
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's insightful comments, which prompted us to provide an in-depth explanation of the synergistic feasibility and potential trade-offs between the two core strategies proposed in this study—enhancing molecular polarizability and maximizing face-on packing—in practical applications. Based on experimental evidence and theoretical analysis presented in the manuscript, we confirm that these two strategies can be simultaneously implemented in practical devices and mutually reinforce each other.
The enhancement of molecular polarizability is primarily achieved through molecular design, such as introducing electron-withdrawing end groups or asymmetric structures to improve the in-plane electronic polarizability of conjugated molecules. This increases the material’s refractive index and extinction coefficient, which not only reduces the optimal absorption thickness of the film but also enhances charge generation and transport efficiency. For example, asymmetric acceptor materials represented by BO-5Cl achieve high polarizability through their unique dual-interface conformation, optimizing charge generation kinetics while reducing non-radiative voltage loss to 0.178 eV [Nat. Commun. 2022, 13, 2598]. Additionally, Hou et al. reported that introducing electron-withdrawing groups into the P3HT backbone significantly increases its electrostatic potential (ESP), which is a manifestation of enhanced molecular polarizability [Chem 2023, 9, 2518-2529]. Greater electrostatic potential energy strengthens intermolecular interactions, thereby facilitating charge generation and transport [Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2021, 60, 15988-15994].
Simultaneously, the strategy of maximizing face-on packing focuses on optimizing molecular alignment orientation. Through methods such as thermal annealing or solvent engineering, molecules can be induced to preferentially adopt an arrangement where the conjugated plane is parallel to the substrate. This orientation not only promotes out-of-plane charge transport efficiency but also aligns the molecular polarization direction precisely with the electric field vector of incident light, thereby enhancing light-matter interactions. Our GIWAXS data clearly demonstrate the synergistic enhancement of optical constants and face-on packing degree in Y6 after thermal annealing. In the reported ternary system PM6:BO-4Cl:BO-5Cl [Nat. Commun. 2022, 13, 2598], the high polarizability and face-on characteristics of BO-5Cl (verified by both single-crystal and GIWAXS analyses) further drove the certified efficiency to exceed 18.2%, providing strong evidence for the synergy of these strategies.
It is worth exploring the potential trade-offs between these two strategies. We found that enhancing polarizability (e.g., through fluorination or chlorination of end groups) is often accompanied by strengthened intermolecular interactions, which promote π-π stacking formation and thereby facilitate face-on packing. Hou et al. also utilized solid additives with strong electrostatic interactions to induce better face-on stacking of NFAs [Chem 2023, 9, 2518-2529]. Furthermore, Table 1 in [J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2024, 146, 14724−14733] reveals a key pattern: an increase in exciton polarizability (Δp) correlates significantly with longer π-π coherence lengths (L ) and higher face-on c orientation ratios, collectively driving improvements in charge transfer rates and internal quantum efficiency (IQE). Although enhancing polarizability and optimizing face-on packing are inherently synergistic rather than conflicting, fine-tuned control remains essential during implementation. For instance, excessive thermal annealing may induce molecular rotation toward edge-on or end-on orientations, slightly reducing in-plane polarizability, but this risk can be effectively mitigated by optimizing process parameters.
In summary, enhancing molecular polarizability and maximizing face-on packing are fundamentally compatible and mutually reinforcing. Any potential trade-offs mainly arise in specific scenarios such as thickness optimization and can be fully resolved through molecular design and process control. Our proposed co-optimization framework (Fig. 7b) leverages the synergistic effect of these two strategies to reduce the optimal active layer thickness, balance device parameters, and ultimately maximize efficiency. Future research will focus on scalable solutions such as designing asymmetric acceptors that integrate polarizability with self-assembled face-on characteristics, thereby advancing the industrial application of this strategy. We thank the reviewer again for their valuable comments, as this clarification further confirms the robustness and universal applicability of our proposed strategies.
We have added a brief explanation “It is important to clarify that these two strategies are not competitive but complementary. Enhancing the in-plane polarizability of materials (for instance, through fluorinated end groups or asymmetric molecular structures) simultaneously promotes charge generation/transport and improves face-on molecular stacking. This dual effect optimizes the thickness corresponding to peak performance in J /FF/V , thereby collectively elevating the device’s PCE. This SC OC paradigm provides critical guidelines for next-generation OPV material development” on Page 25 to further clarify the synergistic relationship between the two strategies for readers.
3. While the study focuses on optical optimization for enhanced device performance, it would be valuable to discuss how such optimization strategies might affect the long-term durability and stability of the devices. Could the authors comment on any potential implications in this regard?
Response:
We appreciate your valuable suggestions. These not only contribute to our deeper understanding of the influence of molecular polarizability on device performance but also provide valuable direction for our future research. Prior to this, we had not fully considered the potential impact of our proposed optimization strategies on device stability.
In our view, the factors influencing device stability are multifaceted. Due to considerations of manuscript length and focus, we do not intend to discuss this aspect further within the current study, to avoid confusing the reader. However, based on reported literature and our current understanding, we can derive hypotheses regarding the potential influence of molecular polarizability and face-on oriented packing on the stability of OPV devices.
Firstly, an increase in molecular polarizability may promote the internal ordering of molecular packing within the film. This could potentially enhance the mechanical stability of the device, which might be beneficial for flexible OPV devices. Secondly, higher molecular polarizability can strengthen intermolecular dipole-dipole interactions, thereby elevating the glass transition temperature and consequently improving the device’s thermal stability. Furthermore, regarding photostability, literature reports indicate that enhancing the electron-withdrawing capability of the end groups in NFAs can effectively improve device photostability. This improvement is attributed to denser molecular packing suppressing triplet state generation and inhibiting molecular isomerization [Adv. Energy Mater. 2022, 12, 2201267]. Additionally, increasing the polarizability of small-molecule acceptors may foster stronger interactions between donor and acceptor materials, leading to the formation of a highly intermixed stable blend morphology and enabling efficient excited-state quenching.
Similarly, methods such as thermal annealing or solvent engineering that enhance the face-on oriented molecular packing within the film can also lead to tighter intermolecular π-π interactions, thereby stabilizing the structure. In summary, we hypothesize that the two strategies we propose (enhancing polarizability and face-on orientation) may be beneficial for improving device stability. However, given that current research on device stability is not yet fully comprehensive, or due to limitations in our current understanding, there is a possibility of unintended adverse effects, such as vertical phase separation induced by differences in surface energy. We plan to investigate this aspect in future work, and we sincerely thank you again for your insightful comments.

Additionally, regarding the suggestion that the S values for all materials should be 2D derived from the pole figure of the backbone peak to ensure a consistent comparison basis, we fully appreciate the rationale. However, as the reviewer correctly noted, obtaining a clear backbone peak signal is challenging for most molecules in our study. The lamellar diffraction peak, however, provides a strong and reliable signal across the dataset.
Consequently, we made the deliberate choice to use the lamellar peak for the S 2D calculation for all molecules, including Y6, to assess the tilt behavior of the molecular assemblies (Fig. 2f). We believe this extrapolation is justified for the following reasons:
1. The lamellar packing signals are strong and highly reliable, whereas the scattering signals from the (001) plane, which directly indicates end-on orientation, are generally difficult to observe.
2. An S value closer to 0 indicates a more isotropic molecular packing (lower 2D crystallinity), which inherently leads to a greater degree of backbone tilting (J. Mater. Chem. A 2023, 11, 26499-26507; Adv. Funct. Mater. 2011, 21, 3697-3705), especially when such changes in S are related to thermal annealing treatment, which is widely 2D recognized as a method that enhances crystallinity.
3. In the case of Y6, which maintains a three-dimensional network morphology in films (Nat. Commun. 2020, 11, 3943) similar to its single crystal, any out-of-plane tilt of the lamellar stacks inherently necessitates a proportional out-of-plane tilt (i.e., towards end-on) of the constituent molecular backbones.
We have thoroughly revised the section “Effect of molecular packing and orientation on reflection intensity” as the following and hope this elaboration meets your approval.
On page 9, “For organic conjugated films, the ultrahigh reflection not only originates from molecular conjugation and film thickness, but also is closely related to molecular packing orientation. As shown in the GIWAXS results in Fig. 2a, the Y6 film exhibits a distinct face-on molecular orientation, with its conjugated plane parallel to the substrate and thus perpendicular to the incident light. Furthermore, the reduced broadening of the scattering signals for the (010), (200), and (300) planes after thermal annealing (TA) treatment generally indicate improved molecular orientation uniformity40,41, and the orientation changes of Y6 molecules can be quantified by analysing the azimuthal variation of the scattering signals. Fig. 2b displays the orientation ratios of the lamellar packing (300) plane for the Y6 film before and after TA treatment, where an azimuthal angle of 90° corresponds to the in-plane direction and 0° to the out-of-plane direction. After TA treatment, the increased ratio at larger azimuthal angles (closer to 90°) and the decreased ratio at smaller azimuthal angles (closer to 0°) demonstrate a higher degree of face-on orientation, revealing enhanced molecular order and crystallinity. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 5, the same phenomenon is observed in the GIWAXS results of other materials before and after TA treatment.
Molecular orientation changes result from rotation along different axes, which in turn leads to variations in light-matter interactions. As illustrated in Fig. 2c, for the Y6 molecular packing configuration after TA treatment, the rotation along the [100] axis induces a “face-on to end-on” orientation transition, while rotation along the [001] axis produces a “face-on to edge-on” transition. For 2D-polarized molecules like Y6, “face-on to end-on” rotation reduces the polarizability projected onto the X-Y plane, thereby weakening light-matter interactions and thus decreasing the reflection intensity. In contrast, for “face-on to edge-on” rotation, the reflection of the molecules is relatively less affected, though still influenced, because the polarizability along the Y-direction is much smaller than that along the X-direction. For 1D-polarized molecules like P3HT, “face-on to end-on” rotation also reduces the polarizability projected onto the X-Y plane, consequently diminishing light-matter interactions. However, due to their 1D-polarization characteristics, “face-on to edge-on” rotation has a negligible effect on light-matter interactions. Besides, regardless of 1D- or 2D-polarization, after TA treatment, most conjugated organic small molecules exhibited an enhanced reflection, and the corresponding reflection curves before and after TA treatment are plotted in Supplementary Fig. 6, where the TA treatment (160 ℃, and higher annealing temperature will affect the composition and flatness, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 7) helps suppress the molecular rotation. As shown in Fig. 2d, the maximum reflection of Y6 is increased from 46.7% to 52.9% after TA treatment, and the maximum refractive index n is also increased from 4.08 to 4.17 (Supplementary Fig. 8).
In fact, based on their molecular structures, polymer donor materials such as PM6 and PBDB-T possess a certain degree of 2D-polarizability. However, their optical constants are nearly identical in magnitude to those of 1D-polarized molecules like P3HT. This phenomenon can be partly attributed to their weaker 2D-polarization characteristics compared to molecules with extended 2D-conjugation, such as Y6. Additionally, these polymers tend to adopt edge-on/isotropic molecular packing orientations, where the molecular y-axis remains perpendicular to the electric field vector of incident light. Consequently, polarization along the y-direction remains inactive, resulting in optical properties that more closely resemble those of 1D-polarized molecules.
The correlation between molecular packing within the film and the film’s absorption/reflection is illustrated in Fig. 2e. For 2D-polarized small molecules like Y6, the high maximum reflection primarily stems from their highly ordered face-on orientation. As mentioned earlier, edge-on rotation causes a slight reduction in the film’s reflection, while end-on rotation leads to a more pronounced decrease. The S 2D parameter, calculated using the formula S = 2⟨cos2γ⟩ − 1 32, can be employed to 2D quantify the degree of out-of-plane orientation from GIWAXS measurements, where γ represents the angle between the molecular backbone plane and the substrate plane normal. An S value between -1 and 0 indicates a preferred face-on orientation, a value 2D between 0 and 1 indicates a preferred edge-on orientation, and S = 0 represents an 2D isotropic orientation. We selected the lamellar packing scattering signals, specifically the (100) plane or its higher-order diffraction for S calculation for the following 2D reasons: (1) The lamellar packing signals are strong and highly reliable, whereas the scattering signals from the (001) plane, which directly indicates end-on orientation, are generally difficult to observe; (2) Improved lamellar packing uniformity leads to a reduction in isotropic molecules, which then infers to a suppression of the end-on oriented molecules that are the primary factor in reflection degradation, thereby resulting in the enhancement of film reflection.40,42; (3) For molecules like Y6 that feature a three-dimensional network-like packing structure, rotation of the lamellar packing plane also implies an increase in the proportion of “end-on” oriented molecules41. We systematically investigated a series of 1D- and 2D-polarized molecules by comparing their S parameters and maximum reflection before and after 2D TA, as shown in Fig. 2f. The TA treatment increases the absolute S value for all 2D molecules, indicating enhanced orientation uniformity, and the suppression of isotropic and end-on molecular rotation, consequently leading to improved maximum reflection. The representative 2D-polarized molecules, including Y6, IT-4Cl, and IEICO-4F, exhibit maximum reflection exceeding 40% with highly face-on orientation characteristics. In contrast, the other molecules shown in Fig. 2f demonstrate reflection below 35%, primarily due to their 1D-polarization optical properties. These results are in strong agreement with refractive index measurements.”
